title: Navigating AI’s Frontier in 2025 - Grace Isford, Lux Capital

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on agent reliability, compounding errors in multi-step autonomous systems, and architectural mitigations like scaffolding, self-healing, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Strategies and examples span multiple verticals rather than focusing on a single application domain. The talk addresses development practices like data curation and evals alongside production concerns like cascading failures and scaffolding at Ramp. Compounding error math, scaffolding, and data flywheels require agent systems familiarity but are presented accessibly for practitioners. Recorded keynote at the AI Engineer Summit 2025 in New York. Classification is based on a venture capitalist's practitioner observations and illustrative demonstrations rather than controlled experiments.

summary: Grace Isford (Lux Capital) opens by introducing Lux's frontier-tech investment thesis and its NYC AI roots, citing portfolio companies like Hugging Face, Together AI, Physical Intelligence, and Sakana AI. She traces the AI hockey-stick growth from Stable Diffusion (Aug 2022) through 2025 milestones: the $500B Stargate project, OpenAI o3 exceeding ARC-AGI performance, DeepSeek R1's disruptive launch, and the France AI Summit. She calls 2025 the 'perfect storm' for AI agents—reasoning models outperforming humans, test-time compute gains, cheaper inference, and narrowing open/closed-source gaps—but cautions that agents aren't reliably working yet, defining an AI agent as a fully autonomous system where LLMs direct their own actions. A live demo of OpenAI Operator failing to book a simple NYC-to-SFO flight illustrates the problem. She catalogues five error types: decision errors, implementation errors, heuristic errors, taste errors, and a perfection-paradox mismatch between magical expectations and inconsistent results. She shows that a 99%-accurate agent drops to ~60% over 50 steps while a 95%-accurate agent diverges by ~50 percentage points. She then outlines five mitigation strategies. (1) Data curation—proprietary, multi-modal, and agent-generated data with a data flywheel. (2) Evals—distinguishing verifiable vs. non-verifiable domains, collecting human-preference signals, and sometimes relying on vibes-based testing. (3) Scaffolding systems—infrastructure to prevent cascading errors (citing Ramp), human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and self-healing agents that correct their own paths. (4) UX—foundation models are the fastest depreciating asset class, so UX and deep workflow understanding differentiate products; examples include Codium (developer psyche), Harvey (legal Legacy integration), and Deep Research (clarifying questions). Lux is excited about companies with proprietary data in robotics, defense, manufacturing, and life sciences. (5) Multimodality—moving beyond chatbot interfaces toward voice, smell (Osmo), touch/robotics, memory, and visual canvases (Tldraw). She concludes that lightning hasn't struck yet, agents won't happen overnight, and cumulative errors remain a core challenge, but data curation, evals, scaffolding, UX, and multimodality are the tools to overcome them.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Tiny cumulative errors—decision, implementation, heuristic, taste, and perfection-paradox errors—compound across multi-step tasks, causing significant accuracy drops.
Strategy 1—Data curation: leverage proprietary, multi-modal, and agent-generated data; design an agent data flywheel that improves with use.
Strategy 2—Evals: differentiate verifiable domains from non-verifiable ones; collect human-preference signals; sometimes vibes-based testing is the best eval.
Strategy 3—Scaffolding: build infrastructure to prevent cascading errors (Ramp example); enable self-healing agents and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
Strategy 4—UX: foundation models are the fastest depreciating asset class; UX and workflow understanding differentiate products (Codium, Harvey, Deep Research).
Strategy 5—Multimodality: move beyond chatbot interfaces toward voice, smell (Osmo), touch/robotics, memory, and visual canvases (Tldraw).

sections.title: Introduction and Lux Capital Overview
sections.summary: Grace introduces herself as a Lux Capital Partner, describes Lux's frontier-tech investment thesis ('believe before others understand'), and lists portfolio AI companies: Hugging Face, Together AI, Physical Intelligence, and Sakana AI (Tokyo).

sections.title: Lux Capital's NYC Commitment
sections.summary: Lux was founded in NYC, made its first AI investment there in 2013, and a majority of its AI portfolio is headquartered or has a major hub there. Lux is bullish on the NYC AI ecosystem.

sections.title: AI Growth Trajectory Since 2022
sections.summary: Traces the hockey-stick growth from Stable Diffusion (Aug 2022) through 2025, noting models are more performant, compute-efficient, and increasingly from diverse labs (xAI, Mistral, DeepSeek).

sections.title: 2025 AI Milestones
sections.summary: Cites the $500B Stargate project, OpenAI o3 exceeding ARC-AGI, DeepSeek R1's disruptive launch (Nvidia shares tumbling, #1 App Store), and the France AI Summit with Macron.

sections.title: The 'Perfect Storm' for AI Agents
sections.summary: Reasoning models, test-time compute, cheaper inference/hardware, narrowing open/closed-source gap, and massive infrastructure investment set the stage for agents—but Grace sees 'a lot of thunder' but no lightning strike yet. Defines an AI agent as a fully autonomous system where LLMs direct their own actions.

sections.title: OpenAI Operator Flight-Booking Demo
sections.summary: A seemingly simple flight-booking query (NYC to SFO, Monday, after 3pm, under $500, aisle seat, preferred airlines) fails twice: first via Kayak (no flight found), then Skyscanner (5:30pm JFK flight, bad traffic, no seat selection).

sections.title: Five Types of Cumulative Errors
sections.summary: Catalogues decision errors (wrong facts), implementation errors (wrong access/integrations), heuristic errors (wrong criteria), taste errors (wrong personal preferences), and a perfection-paradox mismatch between magical expectations and inconsistent agent performance.

sections.title: Compounding Error Visualization
sections.summary: Shows that a 99%-accurate agent drops to ~60% over 50 steps while a 95%-accurate agent diverges by ~50 percentage points, illustrating how cumulative errors compound in multi-step agent systems.

sections.title: Strategy 1: Data Curation
sections.summary: Emphasizes curating proprietary, multi-modal data (web, image, video, audio, sensor, agent-generated). Advocates designing an agent data flywheel from day one so usage improves the product in real time. Uses the flight example: curated personal travel preferences and recycling booking outcomes back into the system.

sections.title: Strategy 2: Evals
sections.summary: Discusses the importance of evals, distinguishing verifiable domains (math/science, e.g., Grok 3 benchmarks) from non-verifiable ones (personal preferences). Cites the deep-research eval debate across OpenAI, Perplexity, and Gemini. Emphasizes collecting human-preference signals and acknowledges that sometimes vibes-based self-testing is the best available eval.

sections.title: Strategy 3: Scaffolding Systems
sections.summary: Discusses preventing cascading errors when one agent failure occurs. Cites Ramp (Lux portfolio company) as having infrastructure logic to isolate failures from cascading across the agentic system and production infrastructure. Advocates human-in-the-loop checkpoints and self-healing agents that recognize errors and correct their own path. Returns to the travel example: adding a checkpoint for the agent to verify traffic conditions.

sections.title: Strategy 4: User Experience
sections.summary: Argues UX is the differentiator that matters: foundation models are the fastest depreciating asset class, and GPT wrappers alone aren't enough. Cites examples of excellent UX: Deep Research asking clarifying questions, Codium understanding developer psychology, Harvey integrating with legal Legacy systems for real ROI. Lux is excited about companies with proprietary data and deep workflow knowledge in robotics, defense, manufacturing, and life sciences.

sections.title: Strategy 5: Multimodality
sections.summary: Argues for moving beyond chatbot interfaces toward truly multimodal experiences: voice (getting 'scary good'), smell (Osmo, a Lux investment digitizing smell), touch and embodiment via robotics, memory and personalization, and visual canvases (Tldraw, a Lux portfolio company reimagining the visual canvas with AI through brushstrokes and a 'head computer' combining multiple AI models in tandem).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Summarizes the talk: 2025 is the perfect storm but lightning hasn't struck; agents won't happen overnight. Cumulative errors—wrong answers, preferences, criteria, and human expectations—abound. Data curation, evals, and scaffolding are mitigation tools. Urges builders to think bigger about UX, multimodality, and innovative product experiences that set workflow and vision apart.

demonstrations: OpenAI Operator flight-booking demo: asked to book NYC-to-SFO flight on Monday with constraints (after 3pm, avoid rush hour, United/JetBlue/American, under $500, aisle seat, before midnight). First attempt went to Kayak and found no flight; second attempt used Skyscanner, found a 5:30pm JFK flight (bad traffic time) but could not pick seat—failed to meet most constraints.
limitations: Agents suffer from decision errors, implementation errors, heuristic errors, taste errors, and a perfection-paradox expectation mismatch
Compound errors are amplified in complex multi-agent systems with multi-step tasks
OpenAI Operator could not handle captchas, wrong integrations, or personal preference constraints
Non-verifiable domains lack clear yes/no answers, making evals harder
Foundation models are the fastest depreciating asset class, making GPT wrappers insufficient for differentiation
Without scaffolding, a single agent error can cascade across the entire production infrastructure
quantitativeClaims: $500B Stargate project announced between US government, OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle
99%-accurate agent drops to ~60% accuracy over 50 consecutive steps
~50 percentage-point gap between 95% and 99% agents after 50 tasks
